title: Treat block size, occupancy, registers, and latency hiding as a joint frontier

source.title: CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide, Execution Configuration Optimizations
source.claim_scope: General NVIDIA CUDA guidance; exact resource limits require official target-device evidence and compiled-kernel resource data.

implementation_recipe: Choose a few block sizes that occupy different resource regimes rather than sweeping every multiple of a warp.
Pair block-size candidates with compiled register/shared-memory usage and active-block estimates.
Include an ILP or coarsening point because lower occupancy can still win when it exposes useful independent work.
validation_recipe: Measure the same candidate over anchor and edge sizes to expose wave and tail effects.
Record final register/shared-memory use and distinguish theoretical occupancy from achieved activity.
Stop when adjacent frontier points no longer change the weighted objective materially.
expected_bottleneck_shifts: More resident warps can hide latency but reduce registers available for instruction-level parallelism.
Larger blocks can improve amortization while worsening tail waves or resource granularity.
failure_modes: The search maximizes occupancy as if it were the objective.
Block size variants compile to materially different register spilling.
The anchor size hides a partial-wave regression.
scope_limits: Occupancy is a mechanism, not a performance target.
Do not copy compute-capability examples into the target hardware model.

candidate_archetypes.name: smaller-block latency-hiding point
candidate_archetypes.template: Implement a 128-thread point and compare it with the current schedule using compiled resource usage and edge-size timing.

candidate_archetypes.name: lower-occupancy ILP point
candidate_archetypes.template: Process multiple independent elements per thread while preserving coalescing, then test whether extra ILP offsets reduced residency.
